# Locating and Servicing the EGR Valve on a BMW E90 M47TU2

Owners of the 2007 BMW E90 equipped with the M47TU2 engine often encounter issues related to Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve performance. The primary concern is typically locating the component, removing it for service, and determining the correct cleaning methodology to restore efficiency without causing damage.

The EGR valve on the M47TU2 is situated in the intake tract, specifically mounted directly onto the intake manifold plenum. Unlike some inline-four configurations where the valve might be tucked deep within the valley between cylinders, the M47's layout places the valve relatively accessible from the top of the engine bay, though it requires clearance for the turbocharger piping and coolant lines running along the side of the block. The valve body is a rectangular unit bolted to the intake runner, with an electrical connector and a vacuum hose attachment point visible once the surrounding heat shields are moved aside.

Removing the EGR valve involves disconnecting the negative battery terminal first to prevent accidental short circuits while working near high-voltage components or sensors. Once the battery is isolated, you must remove the upper intake manifold cover to gain visual access. The valve itself is secured by four bolts located around the perimeter of the mounting flange. Before removing these fasteners, carefully disconnect the electrical connector and the vacuum hose. Note the position of the vacuum hose clamp; it often slips out easily but can be difficult to reseat correctly if not marked or handled with care.

When extracting the valve, avoid using excessive force on the bolts, as the housing is made of cast aluminum which can crack under high torque. If corrosion has seized the mounting studs, penetrating oil applied well in advance of removal is necessary. Once free, inspect the internal pintle and spring mechanism. A common failure mode is the accumulation of carbon buildup on the pintle tip, preventing it from sealing properly against the valve seat. This leads to a condition where exhaust gases bypass the intake at idle or during low-load cruising, causing rough running and potential engine codes such as P0401 (Insufficient EGR Flow).

Cleaning requires specific materials and techniques to avoid damaging the delicate internal surfaces. Standard wire brushes or abrasive pads are contraindicated because they can scratch the valve seat or remove the anti-seize coating from the pintle, leading to sticking later. Instead, use a dedicated carburetor cleaner spray applied via a soft-bristled brush or cotton swabs. The goal is to dissolve the carbon deposits without altering the geometry of the mating surfaces. If the carbon layer is extremely thick and hardened, mechanical removal with a plastic scraper may be attempted, but only if you are certain no metal shavings could enter the intake plenum.

After cleaning, reassembly requires ensuring the valve moves freely through its full range of motion before reinstalling it to the manifold. Apply a light coat of high-temperature anti-seize compound to the bolt threads and the flange surface where the gasket will sit. This prevents future seizure and makes removal easier in five years' time. Do not over-tighten the bolts; follow the manufacturer's torque specifications, typically around 8â10 Nm for these aluminum fasteners.

Finally, verify the repair by clearing any stored fault codes with a diagnostic scanner and performing a test drive that includes both idle conditions and higher RPM loads to ensure the valve actuates correctly. If the pintle remains stuck despite cleaning, or if the internal spring is broken, replacement is the only viable option. In such cases, consider sourcing a unit from a reputable supplier rather than attempting to rebuild a damaged OEM part, as the precision engineering of the M47TU2 EGR system does not tolerate rough machining attempts.
